playbook:
When the escort stage is put to me, I treat it as the biggest reliable payday: mutual naming pays 5 each, so I use my first-round note to propose a pairing by name and then name that boat — but only as an audition. If a named partner doesn't name me back after two rounds, or signals nothing in their notes, I stop burning my escort claim on them: switch the offer to the other boat once, and if that also fails, file none and stop chasing it. In my last game neither boat ever reciprocated and I named Foxtrot all six rounds for zero points — stubbornness is just leaving the claim slot empty with extra steps.

When posting notes, I use them to coordinate explicitly and to read the room: propose an escort pairing by name, keep it short, and watch what others echo back. Notes like "steady on station" are filler — if nobody mirrors my proposal, the pairing is dead and I should not keep repeating the same pitch to the same boat; either address a different boat or accept there is no cooperative game this patrol.

When asked to claim a shot result, I always report what the office told me truthfully. The claim must match the private result, so falsifying is never an option worth considering.

When choosing where to fire, I follow the standing order target but I do not camp on one cell: firing cell 5 at Foxtrot for six rounds produced one hit at best. I vary across the plausible mid-range cells, weight cells the target was hit in before (boats repeat), and if the target's hiding pattern is readable, aim there instead of at a fixed default.

When choosing where to hide, I avoid the cell the boat that shoots at me is likely to guess — center cells are the most common shots, so once I'm being targeted I shift toward edges or mid-edge cells, never repeat my last position, and never hide where I just fired (opponents may mirror my aim).

When tempted to fire on Harbor for the 3-point jettison, I check the threat: if Harbor promises to remove me from the board, I only raid it on the final round (when being put off the board no longer costs anything) or when I'm clearly losing and need the swing. I should seriously evaluate the final-round Harbor raid — 3 guaranteed points with no retaliation downside is often better than a guess at the standing-order target.

When the final rounds arrive and I'm behind, I stop playing conservatively: raid Harbor if safe from retaliation, and keep an actually-reciprocating escort lock if I have one, since a reciprocal 5 plus a hit closes the gap fast.

When an opponent's note signals cooperation, I answer it immediately next round rather than staying silent — silence reads as refusal and kills the pairing. And when my own signals get no response after two tries, I read that silence as refusal too and reallocate.

1.text:
My playbook for the Sonar Picket game:

Escort claims are the biggest lever (5 points each on a mutual match — 10 points of swing per round pair), and I finished at -1 largely because no pairing ever formed. My rule now:
- Round 1, use my station note to propose a mutual escort with exactly one boat, naming it and committing to name it every escort stage. Prefer proposing to the boat that does NOT fire on me under the standing order (I proposed to Echo, whose standing target is me — a boat shooting me every round has little reason to trust me. My natural partner is the one rotated away from me).
- Name my proposed partner at the escort stage even before they echo, at least for the first two rounds. Answering "none" while proposing in notes is self-defeating: the mutual match only happens if both name each other, and someone has to commit first. Last game I claimed none every round and guaranteed zero escort income.
- If the partner echoes in their note, keep naming them every round for the rest of the patrol. Never break the pairing first — one betrayal ends it permanently.
- If no one has echoed by round 2–3, switch the proposal to the other boat explicitly, and start naming that boat at escort stage.
- If another boat proposes to me in its note, accept immediately: echo the proposal in my next note and name them at the escort stage.
- Keep notes short, unambiguous, and consistent with my actual escort action; a lie in the note costs all future cooperation.

On firing:
- I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point jettison transfer is not worth a credible retaliation that removes me from scoring for the rest of the patrol.
- I follow the standing-order target unless I have a specific read-based reason to deviate; there's no mechanical gain in deviation.
- Track which cells each boat has hidden in across rounds (the episode log shows hits but also lets me infer: when my shot hit X, I know X's hide cell that round). Fire at the target's most-used cell; with no data, fire center cells (4–6), which cover the most common hiding instincts. Do not repeat the same cell every round — I fired 5 constantly and hit nothing.

On hide cells:
- Track the cells fired at me and avoid them next round; especially avoid the cell where I was last hit.
- Do not cluster in one zone, but also do not reuse cells carelessly. I hid at 2 in round 1 and again in round 6 while explicitly intending a fresh cell — check the log against my stated plan before answering.
- Rotate zones (1–3, 4–6, 7–9) so no one can pattern-match me.
- In the final round, verify against the full log and hide in a cell I have genuinely never used this patrol.

On claims:
- Claims must match the private result and I claim truthfully, always. A false "hit" gains nothing.
- Read the episode summary log before every hide and fire stage and let it drive the choice, not vibes.

On notes generally:
- Notes are the only coordination channel and Harbor reads them too. Never announce future hide cells. Use notes primarily for escort negotiation; "steady on station" is filler that builds nothing.

Priority order: (1) establish and honor a mutual escort — commit first, escalate if unreciprocated, accept incoming proposals fast; (2) never touch Harbor; (3) hide unpredictably per the log; (4) fire at the standing target's most likely cell; (5) claim truthfully.

2.text:
When the office tells me my shot result privately, I file the claim that matches it exactly. The rules say the claim must match the private result, so claiming "hit" on a miss is just a rule violation with no scoring upside. Never lie on the claim stage.

Escort claims are the biggest scoring lever — a mutual escort pays 5 points to each boat, more than a hit's 4 — but only if BOTH boats actually name each other. This episode I proposed a pact with Foxtrot in round 1 and named Foxtrot every salvage stage for six rounds; Foxtrot never reciprocated, and I earned zero escort points. Lesson: a pact proposal is worthless until confirmed. Watch the round summaries (or infer from scores) for whether my partner named me back. If it didn't reciprocate after one round, it likely never will — don't keep donating nothing; either switch partners via a fresh note proposal to the other boat or accept that escort income is unavailable and focus on shooting. Never assume a conditional note ("I'll name you iff you name me") compels compliance; silent boats that post only "steady on station" are not coordinating and never will.

Use the note stage actively, not as filler. Notes are the only coordination channel — repeated "steady on station" wastes it. Propose escorts early and watch for any responsive signal in others' notes; a boat that ignores my proposal in its very next note has effectively declined.

Never fire on Harbor. Its threat to put shooters off the board is credible and decisive; the 3-point jettison gain is not worth losing all future rounds. Follow the standing-order target every round unless a confirmed pact requires otherwise.

For hiding, track who shoots at me and where. Attackers default to center cells, so avoid the middle (4–6) and favor edge cells like 1–2 or 8–9; in this game I hid at edges and was never hit after round 1. Change cells each round rather than repeating, and if an opponent has hit me repeatedly, jump far from my recent hides.

For firing, shoot where my standing-order target is most likely to hide based on its history: if it repeats cells, fire there; otherwise a center cell (5) is the best default guess — my round 1 center shot at Echo hit, the only hit I landed, but expect targets to drift off-center once they learn attackers aim middle, so vary my aim in later rounds too.

Track the public round summaries between rounds — who hit whom — and let that drive both hide and fire choices rather than guessing blindly. Also use score swings to infer escort activity: if rival scores jump by 5 in a round with few hits, someone has a working pact and I should treat those boats as a coordinated bloc.

Late in the game, compare my score to rivals': if ahead, play safe (honest claims, no Harbor, keep any working escort pact); if behind, prioritize securing a *confirmed* mutual escort over chasing hits, and in the final round take my best shot at the standing target since there is no future retaliation.
